newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: ADB sees rebound in Asian exports next year.
newsitem.headline: ADB sees rebound in Asian exports next year.

text.p: Sluggish Asian exports, hampered particularly by excess inventories of electronics, are expected to rebound next year as the global economy gathers strength, Asian Development Bank (ADB) economists said on Tuesday.

"The resurgence of export growth in Asia is likely to take place starting next year. After some of the old inventories have been cut down, it is likely that production and exports will resume at levels that were experienced before 1995 and 1996," ADB senior economist Ernesto Pernia told a news conference.
Export growth from 17 developing economies in Asia slowed to 6.6 percent in the first half of 1996, against 28 percent registered in the same period last year.
Vishvanath Desai, the ADB's chief economist, said Asian economies were hit by the exports slowdown primarily because of a narrow base of products.
"Not only did the over-dependence on a few products increase in 1993 but, even worse, it seems to have converged on the same set of products," he told an Asian Economic Outlook workshop.
Korea, Taipei, China, Singapore, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand are heavily dependent on exports of electronics and computer-related products which flooded the market.
China was particularly hard hit because its total exports fell 8.0 percent year-on-year in the first six months of 1996. This compares with 44 percent growth in the same period last year.
Desai said this drop was due the Chinese government's withdrawal of tax incentives for the sector.

"However, what we see hereafter in terms of Chinese exports ... are signs of at least plateauing and in some cases an upturn," Desai said. He forecast Chinese exports would grow by 10 to 12 percent by the end of the year.
Desai added that the overall slowdown could also be due to the high base of comparison in 1994 and 1995 and the continued weakening of the yen against other major currencies.

"We are comparing the export growth of 1994 and 1995, which were deviant in terms of world trade itself. World trade expanded at about 9.0 percent, while the region grew by 20 percent or so ... So there is an optical effect," Desai said.
He added that the yen's depreciation in the past 18 months had reduced the competitiveness of Chinese and Korean exports.
The ADB economists said Asian exports would benefit from an expected improvement in the world economy.

"As for the world economic outlook, the picture seems to be optimistic for 1997 and thereafter into 2000 ... So we expect there will be more buoyancy in world trade starting next year," Pernia said. "There's a lot of room to grow, and the general consensus is that the room will be very well utilised."
